taxonomy.subtopic: Fixed splitting of S2 from chronic right-sided volume loading

questions.stem_html:
A 26-year-old woman is evaluated after a soft systolic ejection murmur is noted at the left upper sternal border. She has normal oxygen saturation and no cyanosis. The second heart sound is widely split and changes little with respiration. Echocardiography shows a secundum atrial septal defect with left-to-right flow and right ventricular enlargement.

Why is the splitting of the second heart sound relatively fixed?

options.text_html: The pulmonic valve closes early because pulmonary vascular resistance is permanently reduced
The aortic valve closes late because left ventricular afterload rises during inspiration
Complete atrioventricular block dissociates atrial and ventricular contraction
Right ventricular ejection is chronically prolonged, while respiratory changes in systemic and shunt flow counterbalance each other
An accessory pathway bypasses the atrioventricular node and shortens ventricular filling

questions.explanation_html: A left-to-right atrial shunt increases right ventricular stroke volume and prolongs ejection. With inspiration, increased systemic venous return is offset by reduced left-to-right shunt, so pulmonic closure timing changes little. Counterbalancing respiratory flows preserve prolonged right ventricular ejection across the respiratory cycle, producing fixed wide splitting.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: ASD delays, rather than advances, pulmonic closure due to right-sided volume loading.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Inspiration normally delays pulmonic closure; fixed splitting in ASD is not caused by delayed aortic closure.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: There is no evidence of AV block, and AV dissociation does not explain the characteristic ASD auscultation.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: Preexcitation changes electrical activation, not the respiratory behavior of S2 in ASD.

questions.educational_objective: Explain fixed splitting of S2 in ASD through chronic right-sided volume overload and respiratory counterbalancing of systemic venous return and shunt flow.
